Information from the tabletop and focus groups were then incorporated into a research plan that was vetted by the Community Stakeholder Group, representing diverse community organizations. Neighborhood canvassers were then trained to conduct a survey focused on experiences of grid outages, impacts of outages and different disaster contexts as identified by the CIT, and community preferences for building resilience. Using a three-tier process of community evaluation and input, the team was able to gather a holistic view from all organizations and community household types to prioritize needs, risks, and barriers. By aggregating all of the feedback from the community surveys, focus groups, and tabletop exercises, the results were cross-referenced with the top ten scoring sites from Task 1.0 as further integration of asset-based and community-up approaches. This affirmed Bayview as a primary site for demonstration development because it has one of the highest returns on investment in terms of City operations and budget, critical infrastructure resilience, utility partnership opportunity, community benefits, and energy burden relief for low-moderate income households with appropriate low-income community solar subscription policy implementation. Analysis of the community survey data provided critical metrics on the local context of grid disruptions. While many respondents reported outage durations between 5–12 hours (25.1%) or 2–4 hours (24.6%), a significant minority experienced prolonged losses of power: 1–2 days (16.8%), 3–5 days (14.4%), and over 5 days (4.8%). Further 16 evaluation of this data reflected that those experiencing outages longer than 1 day were nearly evenly split between those impacted by a 2016 windstorm that impacted a part of Duluth and those that experienced the outages while living in other areas. Severe rain/flooding was identified as the most common cause of outages at 16.0%. Other prevalent causes cited included human-caused outages (14.1%), winter storm/blizzard/ice (13.9%), windstorm (13.1%), and extreme cold weather (10.3%), validating the climate-specific focus intended for establishing community-based minimum resilience standards. In addition to developing an understanding of the types of grid disruptions experienced by Duluthians, the neighborhood canvass and outreach strategy worked to identify existing preparedness and willingness of community members to take advantage of offsite community-based response options like shelters. In addition to these door-to- door conversations, a 20-minute survey of 167 individuals was conducted. Survey results substantiated issues identified during focus groups and interviews. Results that informed recommendations on establishing minimum resilience standards included understanding basics like the prevalence of lighting and power sources by individuals that ranged from access to flashlights (89.8%), batteries for lights, radios, etc. (78.4%), candles/matches (74.9%), car charger for phones/small electronics (45.5%), and power banks or portable chargers for small devices (42.5%) to fuel-based generators (15.0%), solar-powered batteries (7.8%), and whole-home batteries (1.2%). In addition, the data on relocation concerns highlighted significant barriers to utilizing centralized emergency shelters. The most frequently cited concern was safety and security (16.8%), encompassing worries about the security of personal belongings left behind and the potential for civil disorder if a person were to relocate during a grid outage.
